opus-5.5.text:
I think right now, for most people, AI is still mostly an abstraction. They've maybe played around with a chatbot, they've seen some headlines, but it hasn't really touched their lives in a concrete way. Their job is the same, their income is the same, the institutions around them work the same way. So when people form opinions about AI today, they're mostly forming opinions about a story they've heard, not about something they're experiencing directly.

Once AI starts having a major economic impact, that changes. If AI systems are automating large parts of the work people do, then suddenly it's not a story anymore. It's about whether you keep your job, whether your wages go up or down, whether your kids have a career path. People care enormously about those things, much more than they care about abstract arguments over capabilities or timelines. So I'd expect the salience of AI as a political issue to go up dramatically, probably to the point where it becomes one of the main things politics is about.

The direction of that shift is harder to call. There will be a lot of people who benefit: cheaper goods and services, better medical care, more wealth overall. But the gains and losses won't be evenly distributed, and losses tend to be more politically potent than diffuse gains. If you lose your job to automation, that's a very vivid, personal grievance. If prices fall by a few percent across the board, you might not even notice it as being caused by AI. So I think there's a real chance of a strong backlash, with demands for restrictions, taxes on automation, protections for particular professions, and so on.

I'd also expect people to update on what AI can actually do. A lot of current skepticism comes from people seeing systems make silly mistakes and concluding that the whole thing is overhyped. When those systems are visibly doing work that used to require skilled humans, that skepticism becomes much harder to maintain. That will cut both ways: people will take the benefits more seriously, but they'll also take the risks more seriously, including concerns about concentration of power and loss of control.

So the basic point is that public opinion right now is weakly held and not very informed by direct experience, and that's exactly the kind of opinion that changes a lot once reality starts imposing itself. I wouldn't put much weight on current polling as a guide to how the politics of AI will look once it's actually transforming the economy.

r001.rationale: The response says current opinion is weakly held and based on little direct experience, and that it may change substantially once AI transforms the economy; it also says current polling is a poor guide to future AI politics.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the basic reason is that right now AI is mostly an abstract thing for most people. If you ask someone on the street what they think about AI, they'll have some opinion, maybe they've used ChatGPT, maybe they've read something alarming in the news, but it hasn't really changed their life in a way they can point to. Their job is the same, their wages are the same, the political system looks the same. So the opinions people hold are kind of cheap. They're not grounded in any strong personal stake.

I think that changes once AI starts automating a large fraction of the economy, which is the scenario I'd expect over the next decade or two. At that point you have people whose jobs are directly displaced, people who see their income going down relative to capital owners, and you also have very visible winners, companies and individuals who are capturing an enormous share of the gains. Historically that kind of distributional shock is exactly what mobilizes people politically. You can look at the industrial revolution, or at trade and globalization more recently. When people feel they're losing out and they can identify who's gaining, you get a backlash, and it tends to be quite strong and quite persistent.

There's also a second channel which is about control and legitimacy. If the systems making important decisions, in government, in the military, in the economy, are increasingly AI systems that ordinary people don't understand and can't influence, I think many people are going to find that alarming regardless of whether the outcomes are good. People care not just about outcomes but about who gets to decide. So I'd expect demands for regulation, for slowing things down, maybe for outright bans in some domains, to become much more mainstream than they are today.

Now, I want to be careful here, because it could also go the other way. If AI delivers very visible benefits quickly, cures for diseases, much cheaper goods, rising living standards, then you might get a lot of enthusiasm, and the political pressure could be in the direction of accelerating rather than slowing down. My honest view is that you'll probably see both at once, polarized along lines that don't map neatly onto the current political divisions. But the thing I'm most confident about is that the current situation, where AI is something elites debate and most people are only mildly interested in, is not stable. Once the stakes become real for people, the opinions will become real too, and they'll be much harder to shift than they are now.

r001.rationale: The response says current opinions are based on AI being abstract and are not stable; once people experience real stakes, their views will become more grounded and may shift toward backlash, enthusiasm, or polarization.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of public opinion about AI right now is fairly abstract. People have impressions based on what they’ve heard, or they’ve used a chatbot a few times, but it hasn’t necessarily changed their lives very much. So I wouldn’t expect those opinions to be particularly stable once the effects become more tangible.

If AI starts threatening your job, that gives you a much stronger reason to care about it. If it helps you get better medical treatment, or makes services you use much cheaper, that’s also a strong reason, potentially pushing in the opposite direction. And different people will experience those effects differently.

So I don’t think there’s a simple prediction that everyone becomes more positive or more negative. I’d expect opinions to become more strongly held, and the political debate to become much more concrete: who benefits, who bears the costs, and what should governments do? Once there are substantial interests at stake, the debate can look very different from the one we have today.

r001.rationale: The response says current opinions are abstract and “wouldn’t expect those opinions to be particularly stable” once AI’s effects become tangible, communicating that present views may poorly predict opinion after substantial impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think public opinion about AI today is formed in a situation where, for most people, it hasn’t changed their lives very much. They might use a chatbot, or see something about AI in the news, but it’s still fairly abstract. Once it starts affecting people’s jobs, their incomes, or the services they can get, their opinions will be based on those experiences much more than on the arguments they hear today.

And that could go in either direction. If people see substantial improvements in medicine or find that AI makes their work easier, that could generate a lot of support. If they see people losing their jobs while the benefits accrue to a small number of companies, that could generate a backlash. Those reactions aren’t necessarily inconsistent: people can appreciate what the technology does and still be unhappy with how it’s being deployed.

So I wouldn’t treat current public opinion as a fixed constraint on what happens in the future. As the stakes become more concrete, people will pay more attention, political coalitions will form, and the questions people are arguing about will change.

r001.rationale: The response says current opinion is not fixed and that people’s views will shift as AI’s effects become concrete, so today’s opinions may not predict views after substantial societal impact.
